annotations.text:
One number leads. Everything else supports it.

'Left to spend' = opening balance + income − bills − expenses − savings − debt. Same formula the spreadsheet dashboard runs.

Two taps and a number.

Keypad first because the amount is what you know. Group and category are one tap each; date defaults to today; note is optional. Logging friction is what kills budget apps.

Meters, not charts.

Spent-vs-budget is a ratio against a limit, so it gets a meter. This one screen replaces the workbook's 28 charts.

Over/under is never colour alone.

Every status carries a sign, a word ('over', 'under') and an icon. Roughly 1 in 12 men can't separate red from green — and 'am I overspent' is the wrong thing to make anyone guess.
All money is Geist Mono with tabular figures, so digits line up down a column. Proportional numerals make a list of amounts look ragged.

Three charts earn their place:

1. Where the money went — sorted bars, one hue, darkest = largest. Not a pie: 20 categories is unreadable as slices.

2. Over and under plan — diverging, centred on zero, because the question is polarity.

3. Net position — a line, only once there are 3+ periods of history.

No dual-axis anywhere.

Matched to FOLO's real tokens: #0B0F17 ink, #10B981 emerald (both already dominant in web/app), #ef4444 for critical, slate greys, Geist + Geist Mono per the @theme block in globals.css.

Field names follow supabase_schema.sql — category_type, budgeted_amount, transaction_date, target_amount.
